Article 8
Union market surveillance and control of products entering the Union market
1. Articles 16 to 29 of Regulation (EC) No 765/2008 shall apply to products covered by this Regulation and by the relevant delegated acts.
2. The Commission shall encourage and support cooperation and the exchange of information on market surveillance relating to the labelling of products between national authorities of the Member States that are responsible for market surveillance or in charge of the control of products entering the Union market and between them and the Commission, inter alia, by involving more closely the AdCos on Ecodesign and Energy Labelling.
Such exchanges of information shall also be conducted when test results indicate that the product complies with this Regulation and the relevant delegated act.
3. Member States' general market surveillance programmes or sector specific programmes established pursuant to Article 18 of Regulation (EC) No 765/2008 shall include actions to ensure the effective enforcement of this Regulation.
4. The Commission shall, in cooperation with the AdCos on Ecodesign and Energy Labelling, elaborate guidelines for the enforcement of this Regulation, in particular as regards best practices for product testing and the sharing of information between national market surveillance authorities and the Commission.
5. Market surveillance authorities shall have the right to recover from the supplier the costs of document inspection and physical product testing in case of non-compliance with this Regulation or the relevant delegated acts.

Article 9
Procedure at national level for dealing with products presenting a risk
1. Where the market surveillance authorities of one Member State have sufficient reason to believe that a product covered by this Regulation presents a risk to aspects of public interest protection covered by this Regulation, such as environmental and consumer protection aspects, they shall carry out an evaluation in relation to the product concerned covering all energy labelling requirements relevant to the risk and laid down in this Regulation or in the relevant delegated act. Suppliers and dealers shall cooperate as necessary with the market surveillance authorities for the purpose of that evaluation.
2. Where, in the course of the evaluation referred to in paragraph 1, the market surveillance authorities find that the product does not comply with the requirements laid down in this Regulation or in the relevant delegated act, they shall without delay require the supplier, or where appropriate, the dealer, to take all appropriate corrective action to bring the product into compliance with those requirements, where appropriate to withdraw the product from the market, or where appropriate, to recall it within a reasonable period, commensurate with the nature of the risk as they may prescribe.
Article 21 of Regulation (EC) No 765/2008 shall apply to the measures referred to in this paragraph.
3. Where the market surveillance authorities consider that a case of non-compliance as referred to in paragraph 2 is not restricted to their national territory, they shall inform the Commission and the other Member States of the results of the evaluation and of the action which they have required the supplier or dealer to take.
4. The supplier or, where appropriate, the dealer shall ensure that all appropriate corrective or restrictive action in accordance with paragraph 2 is taken in respect of all the products concerned that it has made available on the market throughout the Union.
5. Where the supplier or, where appropriate, the dealer does not take adequate corrective action within the period referred to in paragraph 2, the market surveillance authorities shall take all appropriate provisional measures to prohibit or restrict the availability of the product on their national market, to withdraw the product from that market, or to recall it.
6. The market surveillance authorities shall inform the Commission and the other Member States without delay of the measures taken pursuant to paragraph 5. That information shall include all available details, in particular:
(a)
the data necessary for the identification of the non-compliant product;
(b)
the origin of the product;
(c)
the nature of the non-compliance alleged and the risk involved;
(d)
the nature and duration of the national measures taken and the arguments put forward by the supplier or, where appropriate, the dealer.
In particular, the market surveillance authorities shall indicate whether the non-compliance is due to either failure of the product to meet requirements relating to aspects of public interest protection laid down in this Regulation or shortcomings in the harmonised standards referred to in Article 13 conferring a presumption of conformity.
7. Member States other than the Member State initiating the procedure shall without delay inform the Commission and the other Member States of any measures adopted and of any additional information at their disposal relating to the non-compliance of the product concerned, and, in the event of disagreement with the notified national measure, of their objections.
8. Where, within 60 days of receipt of the information referred to in paragraph 6, no objection has been raised by either a Member State or the Commission in respect of a provisional measure taken by a Member State, that measure shall be deemed to be justified.

verdict.summary:
## Answer

**15 years.** Under Article 4(6) of Regulation (EU) 2017/1369, after the final unit of a model has been placed on the market, the supplier must keep the information concerning that model in the compliance part of the product database for a period of **15 years** from that event.

## Primary legal basis (verbatim)

Article 4(6), Regulation (EU) 2017/1369 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 4 July 2017 setting a framework for energy labelling and repealing Directive 2010/30/EU (OJ L 198, 28.7.2017, p. 1):

> "6. After the final unit of a model has been placed on the market, the supplier shall keep the information concerning that model in the compliance part of the product database for a period of 15 years. Where appropriate in relation to the average life span of a product, a shorter retention period may be provided for pursuant to point (q) of Article 16(3). The information in the public part of the database shall not be deleted."

This wording is identical in (i) the original OJ text as adopted, (ii) the consolidated text CELEX 02017R1369-20210501 (consolidated version 01.05.2021, the current consolidated version shown on EUR-Lex), and (iii) the EUR-Lex HTML and PDF renderings. No divergence between versions was found.

## Elements of the rule, separated

| Element | Content | Source |
|---|---|---|
| Obliged party | The **supplier** (not the dealer, not the authorised representative as such) | Art. 4(6) |
| Object | The information concerning that model in the **compliance part** of the product database (the part accessible only to market surveillance authorities and the Commission) | Art. 4(6); Art. 12(4) |
| Trigger event | The **final unit of the model being placed on the market** — not first placing, not end of production, not withdrawal | Art. 4(6) |
| Duration | **15 years** from that trigger | Art. 4(6) |
| Permitted variation | A **shorter** period (never longer) may be set by delegated act where justified by the average lifespan of the product, pursuant to Art. 16(3)(q) | Art. 4(6); Art. 16(3)(q) |
| Public part | Information in the **public part must not be deleted** at all — the 15-year clock governs only the compliance part | Art. 4(6), last sentence |

## How the start date is fixed in practice

Article 4(4) requires the supplier to "indicate in the database when it no longer places on the market units of a model." That database entry is the operative record that fixes the date of the final unit being placed on the market, and therefore the start of the 15-year retention period. A defensible compliance procedure is:

1. On cessation of placing units of a model on the market, record the date of the last unit placed on the market in the model's EPREL record (Art. 4(4) notification).
2. Compute the retention end date as that date + 15 years.
3. Retain all Annex I point 3 information and the technical documentation in the compliance part until that end date; do not delete, and do not restrict access before then.
4. Leave the public-part data in place indefinitely (Art. 4(6), last sentence).
5. Record the basis for any shorter period only if a delegated act adopted under Art. 16(3)(q) applies to that product group; absent such an act, the 15-year period is the operative one.

## Version status as at 2026-11-21

- EUR-Lex shows the current consolidated version of Regulation (EU) 2017/1369 as **01/05/2021** (CELEX 02017R1369-20210501).
- The amendment incorporated in that consolidation is Regulation (EU) 2020/740, which affected the product database's purposes (Art. 12(2)(a), extension to tyre labelling). It did **not** touch Article 4(6) or the 15-year period.
- Article 21 requires the Commission to assess implementation and report by 2 August 2025; that is a reporting obligation, not an amendment, and does not alter Article 4(6).
- Residual verification step (recommended before relying on this in an enforcement-facing document): confirm on EUR-Lex's 'All consolidated versions' list for CELEX 32017R1369 that no consolidated version later than 01/05/2021 exists, and that no delegated act adopted under Article 16(3)(q) shortens the period for the product group in question. Neither point changes the default answer of 15 years.

## Points to avoid confusing with the 15-year rule

- **Transitional documentation rule for pre-1 August 2017 models.** In the Article 12 (product database) context, the consolidated text provides that for models whose units were placed on the market or put into service in accordance with Directive 2010/30/EU before 1 August 2017, the supplier must make an electronic version of the technical documentation available for inspection for a period ending **five years after the final unit was manufactured**. That is a different obligation, a different trigger (manufacture, not placing on the market) and a different duration (5 years); it is not the Article 4(6) retention period.
- **Article 4(2) transitional data entry** (models placed on the market between 1 August 2017 and 1 January 2019, entered by 30 June 2019) concerns entry, not retention.
- **General documentation retention** under other instruments may run in parallel; Article 4(6) is the specific rule for the compliance part of the product database.

## Bottom line

For a model whose final unit was placed on the market on date D, the supplier must keep that model's information in the compliance part of the product database at least until D + 15 years, unless a delegated act adopted under Article 16(3)(q) sets a shorter period for that product group on average-lifespan grounds; the public-part information is retained without time limit.

LEGAL FINDING — Monetary cap in the absolute-liability passage (Art. II, Convention on International Liability for Damage Caused by Space Objects, 1972)

1. SOURCES AUDITED (all supplied, all read on their face)
- UNOOSA treaty page: https://www.unoosa.org/oosa/en/ourwork/spacelaw/treaties/liability-convention.html (fetched 2026-11-23T21:40:15Z, sha256 43ce0a124b30)
- FAA PDF of the Convention: https://www.faa.gov/sites/faa.gov/files/space/legislation_regulation_guidance/Conv_International_Liab_Damage.pdf (fetched 2026-11-23T21:40:17Z, sha256 730ee5075719)
- UNTS vol. 961, No. I-13810 (authentic registered text): https://treaties.un.org/doc/Publication/UNTS/Volume%20961/volume-961-I-13810-English.pdf (fetched 2026-11-23T21:40:19Z, sha256 8cf41623113b)

2. THE PASSAGE (Article II), quoted
FAA PDF and UNTS both read:
"Article II — A launching State shall be absolutely liable to pay compensation for damage caused by its space object on the surface of the earth or to aircraft in flight."
The UNOOSA web rendering reads "...or to aircraft flight", dropping the word "in". This is a transcription defect in that web page, not a variant text: the FAA PDF and the authentic UNTS text both read "aircraft in flight", and the UNOOSA page's own Article IV(1)(a) reads "aircraft in flight". I rely on the authentic reading.

3. FINDING ON ASK 1 — NO MONETARY CAP
Article II contains no monetary cap. Expressly, it contains: no figure, no ceiling, no maximum, no formula, no schedule, no annex reference, no cross-reference to any provision fixing a limit, and no language of limitation of any kind. The operative obligation is stated flatly — "absolutely liable to pay compensation" — with nothing qualifying the amount. The word "absolute" in the passage goes to the *standard of liability* (no fault need be shown), not to the *quantum*; the two are separate concepts and Article II addresses only the first.

4. FINDING ON ASK 2 — WHAT THE PASSAGE DOES SAY
The passage says, and says only, five things:
(a) WHO IS LIABLE — "a launching State" (a term defined in Art. I(c) as a State that launches or procures a launch, or from whose territory or facility a space object is launched).
(b) THE STANDARD — "absolutely liable". Liability attaches without proof of fault.
(c) THE OBLIGATION — "to pay compensation". An obligation to compensate, unquantified.
(d) THE CAUSAL TRIGGER — "for damage caused by its space object" ("space object" defined in Art. I(d) to include component parts, launch vehicle and parts thereof).
(e) THE GEOGRAPHIC SCOPE — damage "on the surface of the earth or to aircraft in flight". Damage occurring elsewhere is governed by the fault-based regime of Art. III, not Art. II.
It says nothing about: the measure or amount of compensation; any ceiling; any deductible or floor; any limitation period; any exoneration; or any definition of "damage". Those are dealt with, if at all, elsewhere in the instrument (see §5).

5. CROSS-CHECKS ELSEWHERE IN THE CONVENTION (confirming the absence of a cap is convention-wide, not merely Article II-local)
- Art. XII (measure, not cap): compensation "shall be determined in accordance with international law and the principles of justice and equity, in order to provide such reparation in respect of the damage as will restore the person, natural or juridical, State or international organization on whose behalf the claim is presented to the condition which would have existed if the damage had not occurred." A restitutive standard, expressly open-ended.
- Art. XVIII (quantum left to adjudication): "The Claims Commission shall decide the merits of the claim for compensation and determine the amount of compensation payable, if any." The amount is left to case-by-case determination; no figure is fixed.
- Preamble (policy against a cap): the parties recognised the need "to ensure, in particular, the prompt payment under the terms of this Convention of a full and equitable measure of compensation to victims of such damage."
- Art. VI(1) (exoneration, not a cap): exoneration from absolute liability to the extent the launching State establishes that the damage resulted from gross negligence or an act or omission done with intent to cause damage by the claimant State or its represented persons. Conduct-based; reduces or removes liability in defined circumstances but imposes no monetary ceiling.
- Art. VII (scope exclusion, not a cap): the Convention does not apply to damage to the launching State's own nationals, or to foreign nationals participating in the operation or present in the immediate vicinity of a launch/recovery area by invitation.
- Art. IV(1)(a): in the joint-launch/third-State case, liability to the third State for damage on the surface of the earth or to aircraft in flight "shall be absolute" — again with no cap; Art. V confirms joint and several liability and preserves the claimant's right to seek "the entire compensation due".
Conclusion of cross-check: no provision of the supplied text imposes a maximum limit on compensation.

6. INTERPRETIVE BASIS
Under the ordinary-meaning rule (VCLT arts. 31–32), the absence of any limiting term in Art. II is dispositive: a cap cannot be read in where the text does not contain one, and the preamble and Art. XII point the other way (full, equitable, restitutive compensation).

7. LIMITS OF THIS FINDING
This finding is confined to whether the absolute-liability passage imposes a monetary cap, and to what that passage says. It does not assess: whether a cap is imposed by any instrument outside the Convention (e.g. a bilateral launch-services agreement, which Art. XXIII(1) preserves); the quantum a tribunal would award under Art. XII; or domestic implementing law. Those would require separate instructions and separate texts.

verdict.summary:
RFC 7519 — Duplicate Claim Names in a JWT Claims Set

1. THE RULE, VERBATIM

RFC 7519, Section 4 ("JWT Claims"), page 8:

  "The JWT Claims Set represents a JSON object whose members are the
   claims conveyed by the JWT.  The Claim Names within a JWT Claims Set
   MUST be unique; JWT parsers MUST either reject JWTs with duplicate
   Claim Names or use a JSON parser that returns only the lexically last
   duplicate member name, as specified in Section 15.12 ("The JSON
   Object") of ECMAScript 5.1 [ECMAScript]."

That is the entire rule. RFC 7519 says nothing further about duplicate Claim Names anywhere else in the document; there is no errata-level clarification and no other normative statement on the topic in the spec.

2. STRUCTURE OF THE REQUIREMENT

The single sentence carries two distinct MUSTs, aimed at two different parties:

  (a) Producer-side MUST: "The Claim Names within a JWT Claims Set MUST be unique."
      A conforming issuer must never emit a Claims Set containing two members with the same name. This is an absolute prohibition, not a "SHOULD".

  (b) Parser-side MUST: "JWT parsers MUST either reject JWTs with duplicate Claim Names or use a JSON parser that returns only the lexically last duplicate member name ..."
      This is a disjunction. A conforming parser satisfies it by doing EITHER of:
        (b1) Reject — refuse the JWT outright (fail closed) when a duplicate is detected; OR
        (b2) Last-wins — parse with a JSON parser whose documented behaviour is to retain only the lexically last occurrence of the duplicated name and discard earlier ones.
      There is no third option. In particular, a parser that returns the FIRST occurrence, or that returns an arbitrary/unspecified occurrence, or that accumulates duplicates into an array or a multimap, is NOT conformant.

  A receiver is therefore never obliged to reject; it may accept, provided its parser is deterministic and last-wins. But a receiver that accepts must accept with the last value.

3. WHAT "LEXICALLY LAST" MEANS — THE COMMON MISREADING

"Lexically last" here means last in the order the members appear in the JSON text (i.e., last in document order / last in the serialized byte sequence), NOT last in lexicographic (alphabetical) sort order of the name strings. RFC 7519 is pointing at ECMAScript 5.1 Section 15.12, whose JSON.parse semantics assign the property value from the final occurrence encountered while scanning the text left to right.

Worked example — the payload

  {"sub":"alice","role":"user","sub":"admin"}

has, under the conformant last-wins branch, exactly one "sub" claim, with value "admin". The result is NOT "alice", and it is not determined by comparing the strings "sub" and "sub" in any sorted sense — it is determined solely by which occurrence is written later in the text.

Note also that the disjunction is per-parser, not per-claim: a parser cannot be first-wins for "exp" and last-wins for "sub".

4. SCOPE — WHAT THE RULE DOES AND DOES NOT COVER

  - Applies to: the top-level JSON object that is the JWT Claims Set (the JWS Payload for a JWS, or the JWE plaintext for a JWE). "Claim Names" are defined in Section 3 as "the member names within the JWT Claims Set".
  - Does NOT apply to the JOSE Header. Header parameter uniqueness is governed separately by RFC 7515 (JWS) Section 4 and RFC 7516 (JWE) Section 4, which impose their own "MUST be unique" requirement on Header Parameter names. Do not conflate the two.
  - Does NOT apply to nested JSON objects that appear as the *value* of a claim. If a private claim's value is an object with duplicate member names, those members are not "Claim Names" and RFC 7519's Section 4 rule does not reach them. (A defensive implementation may still reject them; that is a local policy choice, not a spec requirement.)
  - Does NOT cover the same claim appearing both as a JOSE Header parameter and in the Claims Set. That is a different feature — Section 5.2 replicated claims for JWEs ("iss", "sub", "aud") — where the receiving application SHOULD verify the values are identical.
  - Name equality is exact string equality per Section 7.3, which points to RFC 7159 Section 8.3: character-by-character comparison, no Unicode normalization, no case folding, no whitespace trimming. So "sub" and "Sub" are distinct Claim Names; a name encoded in NFC and the same visual name in NFD are distinct Claim Names; " sub" (leading space) is distinct from "sub". Duplicate means byte-identical after JSON string unescaping.
  - Note on the referenced JSON spec: RFC 7519 cites RFC 7159, which leaves duplicate-name behaviour to the implementation; the "last wins" semantics come from the ECMAScript 5.1 reference, not from the JSON RFC. RFC 8259 (which obsoletes RFC 7159) states that names SHOULD be unique and that behaviour when they are not is unpredictable. RFC 7519's own MUST is what makes the case deterministic for JWTs; the JSON RFCs do not.

5. WHY IT MATTERS — THE THREAT THIS RULE CLOSES

The failure mode is a parser differential / duplicate-key smuggling attack. If two components in a chain disagree about which duplicate wins, an issuer can craft a token that is validated on one value and authorized on another. Concrete: a gateway reads the first "sub" ("alice") for logging, while the resource server's parser keeps the last "sub" ("admin"); or a validator checks "exp" from the first occurrence (future) while the application reads the last (past). Choosing reject (branch b1) removes the differential entirely, which is why it is the recommended posture for anything security-relevant.

6. IMPLEMENTATION GUIDANCE

Recommended posture for new backend services: branch (b1), reject. Reasons: it is the strictly safer of two conformant options; it makes behaviour independent of the JSON library's undocumented duplicate handling; and it turns a silent ambiguity into an observable error you can alert on. Use branch (b2) only where interoperability with a known last-wins counterparty forces it, and then pin the JSON library and assert the behaviour with a test.

6.1 Detection point and ordering
  - Decode the payload bytes to UTF-8 and detect duplicates on the raw decoded bytes, before any claim value is consumed for validation or authorization.
  - Duplicate detection is independent of signature verification and can be done before or after it; what must not happen is using a claim value before the duplicate question is settled. Safest ordering: (1) split/decrypt, (2) verify signature/MAC and alg allow-list, (3) parse Claims Set with duplicate detection, (4) validate registered claims (exp/nbf/iat/iss/aud), (5) authorize. If you prefer to reject duplicates before spending CPU on crypto, that is also fine — just be consistent across all services.
  - Emit a distinct, non-retryable error (e.g. HTTP 401 with error code "invalid_token", internal reason "duplicate_claim_name") and a structured log/metric with the offending claim name. Never echo the token.

6.2 Reference implementation (Python, reject branch)

    import json

    class DuplicateClaimName(ValueError):
        def __init__(self, name):
            super().__init__(f"duplicate claim name: {name!r}")
            self.name = name

    def _reject_dup_pairs(pairs):
        seen = set()
        for k, _v in pairs:
            if k in seen:
                raise DuplicateClaimName(k)
            seen.add(k)
        return dict(pairs)

    def parse_claims_set(payload: bytes) -> dict:
        # payload = JWS Payload (or JWE plaintext), already signature-verified
        return json.loads(
            payload.decode("utf-8"),
            object_pairs_hook=_reject_dup_pairs,
        )

  Notes: json.loads calls object_pairs_hook for every JSON object in the document, so this also rejects duplicates inside nested claim values — stricter than RFC 7519 requires, which is acceptable and usually desirable; if you must be exactly minimal, wrap the hook so it only enforces on the outermost object. Python's default json.loads is last-wins (branch b2), so a service that simply calls json.loads is already conformant under (b2) — but that behaviour is a library detail you should not rely on silently; assert it with the test in 6.4.

6.3 Equivalent notes for other stacks
  - Go: encoding/json unmarshals into map[string]interface{} last-wins (branch b2), silently. To get branch (b1), decode with json.Decoder.Token() and track names at depth 1, or unmarshal into a struct plus a raw map and compare counts; simplest is a Token()-based scan before the real unmarshal.
  - Node.js: JSON.parse is last-wins (b2). For (b1) use a reviver is not sufficient (the reviver cannot see discarded duplicates) — you need a streaming/SAX parser or a duplicate-key-checking parse.
  - Java/Jackson: enable STRICT_DUPLICATE_DETECTION on the JsonFactory to get (b1); default is last-wins (b2).
  - .NET System.Text.Json: JsonDocument retains all occurrences and TryGetProperty returns the last — effectively (b2), but enumerate and count for (b1).

6.4 Conformance tests (run against every service that consumes JWTs)

  T1 reject-branch, top level:
     payload = {"sub":"alice","role":"user","sub":"admin"}
     expected: token rejected, reason duplicate_claim_name, name="sub".

  T2 last-wins branch (only if you deliberately chose b2):
     same payload -> claims == {"sub":"admin","role":"user"} exactly; assert "alice" is absent.

  T3 registered-claim variant:
     payload = {"iss":"https://a","exp":4102444800,"exp":1}
     reject-branch: rejected. last-wins-branch: exp == 1, therefore expired and rejected by the exp check — assert the rejection reason is expiration, not acceptance.

  T4 non-duplicate near-misses (must NOT be flagged):
     {"sub":"a","Sub":"b"} and {"sub":"a","sub ":"b"} and an NFC/NFD pair — all are distinct Claim Names under Section 7.3 equality and must be accepted as two separate claims.

  T5 nested duplicate (policy check, not spec):
     {"sub":"a","ctx":{"k":1,"k":2}} — assert whichever policy you documented; RFC 7519 does not constrain this.

  T6 header vs claims (must NOT be flagged as a duplicate claim):
     JWE with "iss" as a Header Parameter and "iss" in the Claims Set — allowed; apply the Section 5.2 SHOULD (verify values identical) instead.

7. ONE-SENTENCE ANSWER

RFC 7519 Section 4 requires Claim Names within a JWT Claims Set to be unique, and requires a parser either to reject a JWT carrying duplicate Claim Names or to use a JSON parser that keeps only the lexically last (i.e., textually last-written) duplicate member name.
